# Loading vectors fast

An embedding pipeline writes a lot of floats, and the way they reach Postgres decides whether a
load takes seconds or minutes. The ORM, where most code starts, is the slowest way. The lab loaded
the same 50,000 rows of 384-dimension vectors in five ways to measure the difference.

## Five ways in

```
    method   | seconds | rows/s |  MB/s | vs orm
-------------+---------+--------+-------+--------
 orm         |    11.5 |   4347 |   6.7 | 1.0x
 executemany |     8.3 |   6024 |   9.3 | 1.4x
 copy_text   |     6.8 |   7358 |  11.3 | 1.7x
 copy_binary |    0.56 |  89363 | 137.3 | 20.6x
 pgpq        |    1.32 |  37746 |  58.0 | 8.7x
```

- **ORM** `session.add_all(...)` is what the app's ingest does. It is fine for hundreds of rows.
- **Core** `insert()` with a list of dicts uses the driver's `executemany`, which is a little better.
- **`COPY` in text format** prints every float as text and parses it again on the server.
- **`COPY ... (FORMAT BINARY)`** with pgvector's binary dumper sends floats as floats. It is twenty
  times faster than the ORM.
- **[pgpq](https://github.com/adriangb/pgpq)** goes from Parquet to Arrow to the Postgres binary
  format. It has no `vector` type, so rows land in a `FLOAT4[]` staging table, and an
  `INSERT ... SELECT` casts them.

The staging step explains why pgpq loses to plain binary `COPY`, even before the cast. On the wire,
a Postgres array puts a 4-byte length in front of every element, so a `FLOAT4[]` takes twice the
bytes of a `vector`.

Binary `COPY` needs one call to teach psycopg the `vector` type, and then a row at a time:

```python
from pgvector.psycopg import register_vector

register_vector(conn)  # teaches psycopg the vector type, binary dumper included
with conn.cursor() as cur, cur.copy("COPY items (title, embedding) FROM STDIN (FORMAT BINARY)") as copy:
    copy.set_types(["text", "vector"])
    for title, vec in rows:  # vec: a numpy float32 array
        copy.write_row((title, vec))
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Index after, not before

Build the HNSW index once the table is loaded. Maintaining it row by row during a load costs more
than one build over the finished table.
:::

## And back out as numpy

Reading goes the other way: the same table back as an `(n, 384)` numpy array, in three ways:

```
 read back as numpy | seconds | rows/s |  MB/s | vs psycopg_rows
--------------------+---------+--------+-------+-----------------
 psycopg_rows       |    0.53 |  95004 | 145.9 | 1.0x
 copy_binary        |     0.4 | 125512 | 192.8 | 1.3x
 adbc_arrow         |    0.74 |  67889 | 104.3 | 0.7x
```

Binary `COPY ... TO STDOUT`, decoded in one numpy pass, is the fastest. [ADBC](https://arrow.apache.org/adbc/)
does not know `vector` either, so the query casts to `real[]`. That arrives as `list<float>` and
pays the array overhead again. ADBC is still the one to use when the destination is Arrow anyway,
as with Polars, DuckDB or Parquet. For numpy, binary `COPY` is fastest in both directions.

In the lab, `src/examples/bench/pg_copy.py` runs the comparison, and `src/vecio.py` keeps the binary
decoder and the ADBC reader for reuse.
